screens.title: File I/O and Command-Line Arguments
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll learn how C programs persist data by talking to files and how they accept input when launched from a terminal. File input and output gives your program a way to read existing data or create and update files so information survives after the program ends. You will meet the FILE pointer as a stream handle, learn common fopen modes, and practice safe patterns: always check whether opening a file succeeded, read or write using the right functions for text or binary data, and always close files to flush buffers and free system resources. We will also cover command-line arguments: argc and argv let your program receive configuration or filenames when it starts, enabling tools and scripted workflows. Throughout, you’ll see concrete examples such as character-by-character copy, string reading with buffer safety, and converting argument strings into numbers safely. By the end you should be able to write a small utility that reads one file and writes another, handle common errors, and accept filenames from the command line. Consider how this ability turns short-lived computation into reusable, persistent work — what file would you make your program produce first?

screens.title: File I/O and Data Persistence
screens.narratorSegment: File input and output is the mechanism by which a program reads from and writes to files on disk so that data persists beyond the program’s execution. Persisting data means the values produced during a run are stored in a file and can be reused later by another run or a different program. In C, files are accessed through a stream handle called FILE pointer. You don’t manipulate disk blocks directly; instead, you open a stream, use library functions to read or write, and then close the stream to ensure data is flushed to disk. A concrete example is saving user settings: a program can write a small text file with options and read it the next time it runs to restore state. A common misconception is thinking files behave like normal variables; they do not. File operations can fail for many reasons: the file may not exist, permissions may be denied, or a disk may be full. That is why every open should be checked for NULL and every write should be checked for success when possible. Key takeaway: treat files as external resources with failure modes and always code protections around them.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Definition

File I/O: core idea

Files store data so it outlives the program. Use FILE pointers as handles to operate on files safely.

• Files are external resources with permission and existence checks.
• Use fopen to open, check for NULL, then use read/write calls and fclose when done.
• Closing flushes buffers; failing to close can corrupt data or leak resources.
Key Takeaway

Treat files as possibly unreliable. Always check opens and close files to persist data reliably.

Concrete example
Save a settings file named settings.txt with two lines: theme and font size. On startup, read the file to restore user preferences.
Common misconception
Files behave like variables. They don’t. Reads and writes can fail and are subject to external state like file permissions and disk space.
Try this
Open a file in read mode that does not exist. Observe fopen returns NULL and your program should print an error and exit gracefully.

screens.title: Opening Files with fopen()
screens.narratorSegment: Opening a file is the first action in any file-based program, and it has three important parts: choose the correct mode, call fopen with a filename and mode, and check the returned FILE pointer for NULL. Modes like "r", "w", and "a" control whether you read, overwrite, or append. Binary variants add a b for non-text data. For example, open an existing text file for reading with "r"; if it is missing, fopen returns NULL. A practical flow: call fopen, if the result is NULL print a clear error naming the file and return a nonzero exit code, otherwise continue with operations. Check permissions and be mindful that "w" truncates existing files — that is often surprising. A common mistake is to assume fopen always succeeds and skip the NULL test; that leads to undefined behavior when the program dereferences the pointer. Another pitfall is using the wrong mode and losing data: opening a file with "w" when you intended to add content will erase the file's contents. Key takeaway: always choose a mode deliberately and verify fopen’s result before touching the stream.

keyIdea.title: Open safely
keyIdea.text: Pick the correct fopen mode and always check for NULL. Use descriptive errors and avoid accidental truncation.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Process Flow

Open file process

Follow this safe sequence every time you open a file.

  1. Decide mode: read, write, append, or binary.
  2. Call fopen(filename, mode).
  3. Immediately test if returned FILE * is NULL. If NULL, print a descriptive error and exit the action.
  4. On success, perform reads or writes and then fclose.
Common Mistake
Opening in "w" when you meant to read will delete existing contents. Confirm mode intent before calling fopen.
Mode quick reference
"r" — read existing file; NULL if missing
"w" — write and truncate; creates file if missing
"a" — append; writes go to end; creates if missing
Add "b" for binary: "rb", "wb", "ab"
Example snippet
FILE *file = fopen("data.txt", "r");
if (file == NULL) {
  printf("Error: Could not open data.txt for reading.
");
  return 1;
}
// proceed with reads
fclose(file);

screens.title: Character I/O: fgetc() and fputc()
screens.narratorSegment: Character-based input and output is simple and predictable. Use fputc to write single characters to a file and fgetc to read characters. A common pattern is a loop that reads until fgetc returns EOF. Remember to store fgetc’s result in an int, not a char, because EOF is a special negative value. A concrete example is copying a file character by character: open the input file in "r", open the output file in "w", then loop reading characters and writing them until EOF. This pattern is useful for small utilities and when you need precise control over character translation. A common misconception is that using char for fgetc will work; that hides EOF and can lead to infinite loops or incorrect behavior. Also, check return values where applicable and close both files to flush buffers. Below is a minimal but complete snippet for copying by characters; study the cast and the EOF check carefully and test on a small text file to see how line breaks and spaces are preserved. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Code Walkthrough

Copying characters

Read with fgetc into an int, check for EOF, and write with fputc. Close both streams.

#include <stdio.h>
int main(void)
{
  FILE *in = fopen("source.txt", "r");
  FILE *out = fopen("dest.txt", "w");
  if (in == NULL || out == NULL) return 1;
  int c;
  while ((c = fgetc(in)) != EOF) {
    fputc(c, out);
  }
  fclose(in);
  fclose(out);
  return 0;
}
Why use int for fgetc?
fgetc returns EOF as a negative integer. If you use char, EOF can be misinterpreted as a valid character and the loop fails.
Misconception
Character loops are slow for large files. They are fine for small tasks and clear teaching examples; for larger data prefer block reads with fread.
Key Takeaway

Use int for fgetc, test for EOF, and always fclose to flush output.

screens.title: String and Formatted I/O: fgets, fputs, fscanf, fprintf
screens.narratorSegment: When you need to read lines or formatted values, C provides fgets and fputs for strings and fscanf and fprintf for formatted input and output. fgets reads up to a specified number of characters into a buffer and always null-terminates, which helps avoid buffer overflows when used correctly. Always pass the buffer size to fgets and reserve one byte for the terminating null. fputs writes a string without formatting; fprintf formats output like printf but sends it to a file. fscanf allows formatted parsing from a file, but it can be dangerous for strings without width limits. Prefer fgets plus sscanf or strtol for safer parsing, because those functions give you more control and error feedback. A concrete example: use fgets to read a line and then sscanf or strtol to convert a numeric field, checking for conversion errors. A common pitfall is using fscanf with "%s" unbounded — that can overflow buffers. Key takeaway: prefer bounded reads and explicit conversion checks to keep programs robust. String and Formatted I/O: fgets, fputs, fscanf, fprintf means use fgets with buffer sizes and prefer safe conversions to avoid overflows. use fprintf for formatted file output.. In practical terms, reading lines and using formatted i/o safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Code Walkthrough

Reading lines safely

fgets(buffer, size, file) reads at most size-1 characters and null-terminates. Always check the return value for NULL to detect EOF or errors.

char buf[128];
if (fgets(buf, sizeof(buf), file) != NULL) {
  // buf contains a null-terminated line
}

Formatted I/O and conversion

Use fprintf to write formatted data. For parsing numbers, strtol is safer than atoi because it reports conversion errors.

Example: Read a line with fgets and convert a number with strtol, checking the end pointer for errors.
Avoid: fscanf(file, "%s", buf) without width limits; it may overflow buf.
Key Takeaway

Bounded reads plus explicit conversion checks are the safe path for string and numeric input.

screens.title: Binary I/O with fread() and fwrite()
screens.narratorSegment: Binary input and output is useful for non-textual files such as images or compiled data where you want to copy raw bytes without translation. fread and fwrite read and write blocks of data and are commonly faster for larger transfers than character-by-character loops. You open a file in binary mode using a mode such as "rb" or "wb" so the runtime does not attempt text conversions. The basic usage provides a pointer to a buffer, the size of each element, a count, and the stream. Both functions return how many elements were actually processed, which you should check to handle short reads or writes. A concrete scenario: read chunks of 4096 bytes from an input file and write them to output until fread returns fewer items or zero. A common misconception is that binary mode is needed only on some platforms; it is critical on systems that translate line endings or special characters in text mode. Key takeaway: for raw byte copying and performance, prefer fread/fwrite with careful checks of return counts and always match binary modes. Binary I/O with fread() and fwrite() means use binary modes and block reads/writes for raw bytes. check returned element counts to detect partial transfers.. In practical terms, working with non-text data and block operations. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Definition

fread and fwrite

Block reads and writes move bytes efficiently. Use a buffer and loop until all bytes are copied.

char buf[4096];
size_t n;
while ((n = fread(buf, 1, sizeof(buf), in)) > 0) {
  fwrite(buf, 1, n, out);
}
Why binary mode?
Binary mode prevents runtime translations such as newline conversions. It preserves raw bytes exactly as stored on disk.
Common mistake
Mixing text and binary modes across platforms may corrupt files. Choose the right mode and match it across read/write operations.
Key Takeaway

For raw data and speed, use fread/fwrite in binary mode and check element counts to handle partial transfers.

screens.title: Closing Files, feof(), and ferror()
screens.narratorSegment: Properly closing files completes the data flow and avoids resource leaks. fclose flushes output buffers and releases the underlying file handle. After reading or writing, always call fclose for every stream you opened. To detect unusual conditions while operating, use feof to test whether the end of the file has been reached and ferror to detect input and output errors on the stream. feof returns nonzero if the end of file has been reached by a previous read; it does not predict future reads. ferror indicates if an error occurred on the stream, such as a hardware problem or write failure. A common misuse is reading until feof becomes true instead of checking the read function’s return value; this can lead to processing an extra invalid read. The safe pattern is to loop while your read function indicates success and afterwards use feof and ferror to decide if the loop ended normally or due to an error. Key takeaway: close every file and use read-return-values plus feof and ferror to distinguish normal completion from failure. Closing Files, feof(), and ferror() means always fclose streams. use read return values first, then feof and ferror to diagnose normal eof versus an error.. In practical terms, finalize operations and detect end-of-file or errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Always fclose streams. Use read return values first, then feof and ferror to diagnose normal EOF versus an error.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Process Flow

Successful completion

Loop on read return values. After the loop, use feof and ferror to check why it ended, then fclose the file.

• Use read return values to control loops rather than feof alone.
• After the loop, if feof is true then you reached end-of-file normally.
• If ferror is true, an I/O error occurred and should be reported.

Example pattern

int c;
while ((c = fgetc(file)) != EOF) {
  // process c
}
if (feof(file)) {
  // normal EOF
} else if (ferror(file)) {
  // handle error
}
fclose(file);
Key Takeaway

fclose matters for correctness. Use read-return-values then feof/ferror to determine success or failure.

screens.title: Command-Line Arguments: argc and argv
screens.narratorSegment: Command-line arguments let a user or script pass information to a program at launch, so the same executable can work on different files or behave differently based on flags. In C, main can be written to accept two parameters: an integer argument count and an array of strings. argc contains the number of tokens passed, including the program name, so running a program with two additional words yields argc equal to three. argv holds the arguments as strings: argv[0] is the program name, argv[1] is the first user argument, and so on. A practical example is a file-copy utility that expects two arguments: input filename and output filename. Always validate argc before accessing argv indexes to avoid out-of-bounds access and undefined behavior. Also remember that argv elements are strings; to use numeric arguments convert them with functions like strtol and check conversion success. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 2.3 › Hands-on Lab
Starter code for a simple copy program. Note the explicit argc check and error paths that close any already-opened streams.
#include <stdio.h>
int main(int argc, char *argv[])
{
  if (argc != 3) {
    printf("Usage: %s <input> <output>
", argv[0]);
    return 1;
  }
  FILE *in = fopen(argv[1], "r");
  if (in == NULL) { printf("Error: Could not open %s.
", argv[1]); return 1; }
  FILE *out = fopen(argv[2], "w");
  if (out == NULL) { printf("Error: Could not open %s.
", argv[2]); fclose(in); return 1; }

  int c;
  while ((c = fgetc(in)) != EOF) {
    fputc(c, out);
  }

  fclose(in);
  fclose(out);
  printf("File copied successfully.
");
  return 0;
}
Try compiling and running with different argument counts and file names to see the error handling. For binary-safe copies open both files with "rb" and "wb" and consider using fread/fwrite for performance.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safer Alternatives
screens.narratorSegment: This slide contrasts common unsafe patterns with safer alternatives. First, some learners call fopen and assume success. Safer: check the pointer against NULL and print a meaningful error before using the stream. Second, using fscanf with unbounded string formats can overflow buffers. Safer: use fgets and then parse safely with sscanf or strtol while checking the result. Third, using char for fgetc’s return value hides EOF. Safer: use int and compare to EOF. Fourth, mixing text and binary modes or using "w" when you intended to append can accidentally destroy data. Safer: choose modes deliberately and prefer append when you mean to retain existing content. Fifth, forgetting to fclose leads to data loss when buffers are not flushed. In this lesson we’ll learn how C programs persist data by talking to files and how they accept input when launched from a terminal. File input and output gives your program a way to read existing data or create and update files so information survives after the program ends. You will meet the FILE pointer as a stream handle, learn common fopen modes, and practice safe patterns: always check whether opening a file succeeded, read or write using the right functions for text or binary data, and always close files to flush buffers and free system resources. We will also cover command-line arguments: argc and argv let your program receive configuration or filenames when it starts, enabling tools and scripted workflows. Throughout, you’ll see concrete examples such as character-by-character copy, string reading with buffer safety, and converting argument strings into numbers safely. By the end you should be able to write a small utility that reads one file and writes another, handle common errors, and accept filenames from the command line. Consider how this ability turns short-lived computation into reusable, persistent work — what file would you make your program produce first?

By the end of this chapter you will understand four practical skills that make small C programs more useful. First, you will understand why file input and output exists: it provides data persistence so results survive after a program ends. You will be able to open, read, write, and close files using the standard C library and choose appropriate modes for text or binary data. Third, you will learn to detect and handle common file errors such as a failed open, end-of-file conditions, and read/write errors; these checks prevent crashes and data loss. Fourth, you will parse command-line arguments with argc and argv so your programs accept filenames and flags from the terminal. Each objective includes hands-on checks and small examples so you can practice immediately. For instance, you will open a file, test the returned pointer against NULL, and either proceed or report an error. These skills let you build utilities that integrate with scripts, work with real data, and avoid common runtime pitfalls. Which objective do you want to practice first?

This second objectives slide focuses on hands-on practice and common mistakes to avoid. You will practice checking fopen return values and closing files to avoid leaks and data loss. You will run small programs that take filenames as command-line arguments and see how different argc values change program behavior. The module highlights buffer safety when using string input functions: always supply a buffer size to prevent overflows when reading lines. You will also practice parsing numeric arguments and learn why functions that report conversion errors are safer than simple converters. For every exercise there is an explicit error path: what to print and when to exit. Practicing those error checks prevents undefined behavior and segmentation faults. Finally, you will complete a file-copy lab that demonstrates all steps in one flow: open input, handle failure, open output, copy by reading and writing, and close both files. These exercises build habits that make your tools robust in real environments.

File input and output is the mechanism by which a program reads from and writes to files on disk so that data persists beyond the program’s execution. Persisting data means the values produced during a run are stored in a file and can be reused later by another run or a different program. In C, files are accessed through a stream handle called FILE pointer. You don’t manipulate disk blocks directly; instead, you open a stream, use library functions to read or write, and then close the stream to ensure data is flushed to disk. A concrete example is saving user settings: a program can write a small text file with options and read it the next time it runs to restore state. A common misconception is thinking files behave like normal variables; they do not. File operations can fail for many reasons: the file may not exist, permissions may be denied, or a disk may be full. That is why every open should be checked for NULL and every write should be checked for success when possible. Key takeaway: treat files as external resources with failure modes and always code protections around them.

Opening a file is the first action in any file-based program, and it has three important parts: choose the correct mode, call fopen with a filename and mode, and check the returned FILE pointer for NULL. Modes like "r", "w", and "a" control whether you read, overwrite, or append. Binary variants add a b for non-text data. For example, open an existing text file for reading with "r"; if it is missing, fopen returns NULL. A practical flow: call fopen, if the result is NULL print a clear error naming the file and return a nonzero exit code, otherwise continue with operations. Check permissions and be mindful that "w" truncates existing files — that is often surprising. A common mistake is to assume fopen always succeeds and skip the NULL test; that leads to undefined behavior when the program dereferences the pointer. Another pitfall is using the wrong mode and losing data: opening a file with "w" when you intended to add content will erase the file's contents. Key takeaway: always choose a mode deliberately and verify fopen’s result before touching the stream.

Character-based input and output is simple and predictable. Use fputc to write single characters to a file and fgetc to read characters. A common pattern is a loop that reads until fgetc returns EOF. Remember to store fgetc’s result in an int, not a char, because EOF is a special negative value. A concrete example is copying a file character by character: open the input file in "r", open the output file in "w", then loop reading characters and writing them until EOF. This pattern is useful for small utilities and when you need precise control over character translation. A common misconception is that using char for fgetc will work; that hides EOF and can lead to infinite loops or incorrect behavior. Also, check return values where applicable and close both files to flush buffers. Below is a minimal but complete snippet for copying by characters; study the cast and the EOF check carefully and test on a small text file to see how line breaks and spaces are preserved. What happens if you try this on a binary file opened in text mode?

When you need to read lines or formatted values, C provides fgets and fputs for strings and fscanf and fprintf for formatted input and output. fgets reads up to a specified number of characters into a buffer and always null-terminates, which helps avoid buffer overflows when used correctly. Always pass the buffer size to fgets and reserve one byte for the terminating null. fputs writes a string without formatting; fprintf formats output like printf but sends it to a file. fscanf allows formatted parsing from a file, but it can be dangerous for strings without width limits. Prefer fgets plus sscanf or strtol for safer parsing, because those functions give you more control and error feedback. A concrete example: use fgets to read a line and then sscanf or strtol to convert a numeric field, checking for conversion errors. A common pitfall is using fscanf with "%s" unbounded — that can overflow buffers. Key takeaway: prefer bounded reads and explicit conversion checks to keep programs robust. The basic usage provides a pointer to a buffer, the size of each element, a count, and the stream.
